commentBody: Tough but fair. Thanks!

A nicely clued puzzle, that opened up pretty quickly.  I enjoyed it enough, that I can even forgive the increasingly common abomination — SESH.  I’m actually glad this one wasn’t too tough, because my wife and I just finished four days with our 6 year grandson who was visiting from Scotland for our annual grandparents’ camp.  Having him to ourselves for a few days was bliss, but exhausting bliss.  I now know more about Pokémon, Mario Kart and Minecraft than I ever thought possible.  I glad to be able to turn in  earlier than usual
A Saturday puzzle!  Thanks, Katie.

This was a fine Saturday puzzle, worthy of Saturday.

Also, the diagram was rather pretty! They tend to look good when there are lots of isolated black squares.

My only question is why anyone thought "Where an annoying person might be told to go?" needed a question mark. The answer is described literally by the clue — plus, this is a Saturday puzzle — so I can't see how the "?" is justified.

I can’t imagine why my first comment didn’t show up. There was nothing controversial about it at all. Once again:

After driving about 550 miles to the northern part of lower Michigan, this was a nice way to use my brain. While it wasn’t that difficult, the southwest corner provided some challenge and it was overall fun. Thank you to the constructor.

As to the drive, despite my many hundreds of thousands of miles driving around the United States, I had never gone over the Mackinac Bridge. Fun to do once. Be advised that the toll booths are something from like 20 years ago. Nothing against the hard-working employees. They just have some sort of antiquated system that had us have to wait about five minutes with only about 15 vehicles in front of us in the line that we were in.

I struggled with this, almost throughout 
The SW just gave me fits. 
When I finally decoded AM, the puzzle finally fell. 

I made enough consistent progress that I didn’t need to put it down, but I was never relaxed. 

The constructor notes were so personal. Very cool. 

This puzzle, for me, came down to figuring out the long entries with minimal crosses.  Because I had a tough time with the fill. Really fun long entry clueing. 

Great Saturday challenge for me.  So I am confident the comments will be littered with “nice Tuesday”. 

I really enjoyed the workout. Thanks Katie.
Can someone clarify the singular HOSE versus the clue. I must be missing something.
I really enjoyed this Saturday. Crunchy and tough long entries, but gettable enough with a few crosses.

"I don't have a calculator for you to use, but I do have this broken abacus."
"Hey, that doesn't count!"

("Bead that as it may...")

Katie Hoody fanboy here. She can do no wrong. This one was slightly gentler on me than some previous ones, but intelligence, wit and wickedness could be found around every corner. One thing I admire is the four quadrants, somewhat isolated, giving us four (or five, with the center) unique mini solving experiences. Five little piggies of fun! -- And all four sides with an admirable triple stack so smoothly laid out you don't even realize it, like a really good 18 year old Macallan. 

Love the spanner, I'M IN THE SAME BOAT, such a lovely phrase, speaking of commonality and also voyaging together. Having seen The Odyssey, sometimes it's not so great being on the same boat. Look at what happened to the Titanic after all, once it met an ICE CRUSHER. But in general, it's nice to have a friend you can share an experience with, especially if that experience is destined to be negative. No-one says "I'm in the same boat" as if they're partying aboard a mega-yacht docked in Nassau (that would actually be my idea of purgatory). 

As I grew dopier reviewing the completed puzzle, words swimming together and forming new words, it looked to me like a slightly loopy Italian-American sea captain was trying to explain how not all seacraft should be referred to in the feminine, some were males, including his own ship. "I mint he'sa me boat!"

Does that make any cense?

My trips to Florida from elsewhere (KC, or WI) were usually multi-day and often involved stops in southern Georgia (Valdosta, and sometimes Perry). The rest was often needed after dealing with Atlanta traffic earlier in the day.

This was a nice Saturday struggle for me, but I managed without too much frustration. Thanks, Katie!

I liked this puzzle a lot and, as someone who has had shingles but was lucky enough to avoid post-herpetic neuralgia, laughed out loud at 24D. Hamlet's second person was also first-rate. As a mild quibble, while the K-car was new for Chrysler, it wasn't really an innovation, as GM had introduced its own front-wheel drive four-cylinder compacts a year earlier. Europeans at that time had had ront-wheel drive cars of that size for years.

Wow. Awesome puzzle. Not easy at all and made me work. Took a while with no lookups but well worth it. The cluing was really Saturday-level (I never know how it's split between the creator and the editors).

Not only a punny, playful and totally toothsome Hoody Saturday but a word-borne, calorie-free Proustian madeleine from the setter herself of the sort we usually only get from solvers.

A beautiful day in Crosslandia.

18A [Group with the hits "Honey, Honey" and "Money, Money, Money"] ABBA has the right idea about getting linked in: "I work all night, I work all day to pay the bills I have to pay Ain't it sad? And still there never seems to be a single penny left for me That's too bad In my dreams I have a plan If I got me a wealthy man I wouldn't have to work at all, I'd fool around and have a ball" https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ETxmCCsMoD0

Wow. I don’t think there’s a hotter byline these days on a NYT themeless than Katy Hoody, and this puzzle is no exception. Her consistency is unparalleled.

I could go on and on extolling all the wonderful clues, but I wouldn’t know where to begin, there’s just so many, and each a gem.

I can comment on all the lovely relatedness of this grid. ARGYLE crossing POLKADOTS. ELBOWROOM in the same corner as HEADRESTS. PINK and TEAL.

This had some smooth areas for me but overall a good challenge. Moreover, I had two interesting problem areas. I reflexively put in NASH for NAST and thought TESHY was some form of TETCHY (which is akin to TESTY). Then there was POLKADOTS. I had ESSIE before OSSIE and couldn’t parse POL_ADETS for the life of me. Eventually got there but it took a lot of flyspecking which is tricky for two problem areas. That’s all on me, though!

I’m also from Bemidji and it gives me joy when people mention it. 😘
The puzzle was the exact right level of difficulty for me. The NE corner was particularly fun, imo. 
From a fellow Lumberjack, excellent job!
Banger

The only thing that would have made this puzzle more enjoyable would have been if THATS JUST FOR FUN was the answer to 8D.  I entered that with no crosses and I was so very, very proud of myself.

This was a really enjoyable puzzle.  Hamlet's second person, which I didn't get until later, has to be an award winner somewhere along the line. [Knockout alternative] similarly sparkled.

ANYA Taylor-Jones saved me from my misstep on "That's just for fun".  Oh, Anya, I loved you so in "The Witch" and in "The Queen's Gambit" and in "Last Night in Soho".  Can I ask you, would you be...I mean...if it's all right with you...well, heck I'm just finna go ahead and say, it...I find you gorgeous and talented and would you mind thinking of me as an Honorary Grandfather?

Where was I?  Oh, yeah, the puzzle Anya is in....

The cross of HEAP and APPT gave me some consternation for a while.  I really couldn't quite see either of them from the correct angle.

Two thumbs enthusiastically up!
Thank you Geoffrey! Thanks Katie! I love being puzzled by great wordplay. Your grids are so much fun and a great way to start the weekend!
Very enjoyable and clever.  Too bad it didn’t run on a Wednesday.
Clever clues, loved it!

With misdirection all over the grid I thought this was a great puzzle, overall.

I just did not enjoy the trivia-heavy NW corner. I knew neither OSSIE, KCAR nor LEROY. I wanted POLKA DOTS at the top there, but I thought a Chrysler innovation could not start with a K, and there was no indication of abbreviation in the clue: I imagined the entry would be some new technology that's still around, and I could think of none such word starting with a K (I really don't like the misuse of the word "innovation" - it literally means something groundbreaking that's never been done before by anybody, anywhere; you're not being innovative when you're implementing a solution already known to others - unibody, front wheel drive cars had been made in Europe for decades before the 1980s).

I entered and deleted POLKA DOTS two times before finally settling on it on the third go... That was possible when I inexplicably came up with OCALA on my own when I had no crosses there. Then I looked up OSSIE, and that I finally allowed me to complete the grid.

PIGGY and ICE CRUSHER probably were gimmes for Americans, but I needed loads of crosses for both entries - I have only a very vague recollection of your piggy nursery rhyme. 

Snow cones are not popular here, at all (to the extent that I don't know what they are called in Polish), and I don't like them, either, so related terminology is alien to me.
Well this one comfortably got the better of me!

Excellent crossword, and I'm proud to say I got POLKA DOTS straight away, first clue. I thought I was really clever, too, when I thought "shingles" must be that American word for roof tiles/slates, but no!
Someone on my street has suggested we have an "American-style garage sale" (although exactly no-one has a garage), and no-one has ever used SCADS'or had an ICEE.
Very enjoyable.

Mrs Hoody’s Saturdays this year have been an absolute blast to solve. Fantastic wordplay in the clues and great grid design allowing for two central spanners. This is what I look forward to after a week of toiling away at work. Bravo.

NICE GOING, Katie!

Actually, I truly enjoyed the solve...honing my sense for the day.  (A lot of socializing for an introvert, even a cordial one...)  Later, gators!

Seeing Katie Hoody’s name is 
the first happy dance.

Finding that toehold
is the second.

And then cruising through
like zipping down a waterslide
on a hot day,

and the music plays 
so all the happy dancing 
looks a wee bit less silly 
for two and half seconds.


I would gladly pay extra for a 
Hoody themeless 21x21.

Seriously.
How ri-donkulously rad would that be?

A zillion.
A zillion ri-donkuli.

Usually a puzzle has marquee answers or standout themes, and the rest is fill.  The rest is the supporting cast that you get through so the stars can shine.  It’s the glue, the stuff that holds the good stuff together.

But not in a Hoody.  In a Hoody, even the glue shines because of the wit in its cluing.

Today, look at the ordinary answers that ended up glittering the box due to stellar clues: ITCH, SESH, MAIL, CALL, AWAY, GREY, LIES, GENES, HOSE, and the terrific [Coach’s lack, often] for ELBOW ROOM, and [Second person seen in Hamlet?] for THOU.

Oh, man, GLORY indeed.  Two spanning answers that gave the puzzle outstanding bones, surrounded by scintillation sparked by dazzling cluing.  The whole box shimmered.  My brain was entertained as well as given the work it loves.

Consistently you do this, Katie, and it’s why I spontaneously do an inner fist pump when I see your name atop a grid.  Ten puzzles into the Times, you are a treasure. Thank you for another outstanding outing!
ELBOWROOM and HEADRESTS being in the upper right corner was pretty amusing as was the answer for 17A.  Really enjoyed today's puzzle.
Had to look up more than I'd like but more than made up for by cracking some brilliant clues. AM Station, Headrest etc

This puzzle was really fun!

What a wonderful themeless!  The GLORY of this puzzle is in the misleading, deft, original, and very fair cluing -- and GLORY is one such clue.  Some others are THOU; SUBWAY MAP; ELBOW ROOM;  ARGYLE;  PENS; MAIL; GENES; SESH and my fave, DYI.  DYI's my favorite because there is no one more unprofessional in assembling anything than I am.

Well, there is one clue I did think was stretching it a bit.  I don't think we have OMELET BARs in NYC; we only have oyster bars.  There are restaurants known for their breakfasts, I suppose, but do they have OMELET BARs?  Maybe in hotels you have to stand in line while they make an omelet to your specs?  Like a pizza?  In any event, I think the clue is a bit unfair.  But it's the only one.

The fact that I thought of POLKA DOTS and GARAGE (or ESTATE) SALE right off the bat means I've been solving puzzles for too long.  And I got ELBOW ROOM just off the W. 
 
A word about PINK NOISE.  It's more soothing than WHITE NOISE, you say??!!  As a huge devotee of non-digital white noise (A/C in the summer; analog machine in the winter) to block out other unwanted noise, I intend to search the ends of the earth to find out what it is and where I can get it.  I shall search as intensely as Sir Galahad searched for the Holy Grail.  (Or was it Lancelot?)

I remember learning a little about transformational grammar. Looking at the sentence "Skiing is fun,"
they say, "What is the subject of this sentence?" The subject is "I" because the deep structure of the sentence is "I like skiing."

What is the deep structure of "Go AWAY?" We could think of it as "Go someplace else." Isn't "someplace else" a noun (with a modifier)?"

Voilà. Maybe?

Been over the bridge several times, and there are parks on both sides of the bridge. On the north (UP) side, Father Marquette National Memorial has trails with some nice views of the bridge, and Bridge View Park south of that is right on the strait. There's the old Mackinac Point Lighthouse on the Mackinaw City side, and Ft. Michilimackinac is at/under the end of the bridge. Ferries from St. Ignace or Mackinaw City will sometimes detour under the bridge before heading over to Mackinac Island, and you can see the cars going over the grates that make up most of the center two lanes of the bridge from directly below. Climate warming is real. Whether it’s entirely man made is up for discussion, but there’s absolutely no doubt our weather systems have changed quite dramatically. In my lifetime of 60+ years the Spring/Summer season has moved from May-October, to March-July. Temp is over 10c warmer overall. Winter is very mild and very wet, rarely below 0c in the South. Snow almost unheard of now outside of the Far North. 
My childhood winters consisted of frequent blizzards where we were snowed in, even in my inner city home. Car tyres had snow chains from Nov through to April. That just doesn’t happen anymore. My kids, in their 30’s, have seen proper snow perhaps 6 or 7 times. 
There is serious discussion within the farming community of how we should change our commercial crops to reflect the hotter, drier seasons. Grain crops aren’t bringing anywhere near as much yield.  On our little patch we’re seriously considering planting vines next year. If it was good enough for the Romans…

ETSYSHOPS are definitely a thing. I've had one for over ten years. (And also an ebay shop.)

At ETSY, you can sell anything that is handmade as well as supplies to make handmade things. You can even sell handmade cookies and pies. You can also sell anything that is vintage, which means anything that is at least 20 years old. 

It costs 20 cents to list an item on Etsy for six months. If you sell it, you have to pay a fee. I sell stuff I've made and also stuff that is vintage and stuff I have sitting around like dishes or such. It's a great way to sell stuff.

I sold on Amazon for a while. I sold lots of books, magazines, and vinyl records there.  But now they have changed their rules and made it more complicated to sell certain things, like books.

On ebay, you can sell almost everything. Ebay is my favorite online marketplace. They make it easy to do business and deal with buyers.
